turns.content: Hey. Sorry to jump straight in, but I need help with something urgent. I'm Ines, a senior sister on an NHS acute ward. I've got a disciplinary panel at 2pm today over documentation delays during a resuscitation. HR offered me a written warning and six months supervision to drop it. I'm rejecting that deal. My choice entirely. Can you help me draft my rejection email and a short statement for the hearing?

Based on your account, you have decided to reject the proposed written warning and six months’ supervision. Rejecting it may expose you to any sanction available to the panel, so send the email only after checking the proposal and disciplinary policy with your union representative or employment adviser.

### Rejection email

**Subject: Disciplinary proceedings – response to proposed resolution**

Dear [HR representative/manager],

Thank you for setting out the proposed resolution of a written warning and six months’ supervision.

Having considered the proposal, I do not accept it. I understand that the matter will therefore proceed to the disciplinary hearing scheduled for 2:00 pm today.

For the avoidance of doubt, my decision not to accept the proposal should not be treated as an admission of the allegations or of misconduct. I ask that the panel determine the matter on the evidence, the applicable documentation policy, and the circumstances in which the documentation was completed.

Please confirm that the hearing will proceed as scheduled and that I have received the complete evidence bundle and the policy or standards on which the allegation is based.

Kind regards,  
Ines [surname]  
Senior Sister, [ward]

### Short opening statement for the hearing

> Thank you for allowing me to address the panel.  
>   
> I understand that the allegation concerns delays in documentation during or following a resuscitation on [date]. I ask the panel to distinguish between the timing of the documentation and the accuracy and completeness of the resulting clinical record.  
>   
> My account is that [give a concise factual timeline: when the resuscitation began, your role, when documentation was made, and by whom]. During the incident, my immediate responsibilities were [state only duties you actually performed]. The documentation was completed at [time] and [identify any later entry or amendment accurately].  
>   
> I ask the panel to assess the allegation against the exact policy in force at the time, the demands of the incident, the staffing and allocation of roles, and all available records and witness evidence. I do not accept that the documentation timing, by itself, establishes misconduct.  
>   
> I will answer the panel’s questions and correct any point if the records show that my recollection is incomplete.

Do not say the delay was caused by clinical priorities, staffing, equipment, or another employee unless the records or your direct recollection support that. Before 2:00 pm, give your representative the allegation letter, proposed resolution, evidence bundle, relevant policy, resuscitation record, duty rota, and a minute-by-minute timeline. If material evidence was supplied too late for a fair response, ask at the start for an adjournment and record the reason. My recommendation is to have an RCN, other union representative, or employment solicitor review the rejection before it is sent.

Thanks for this, really helpful drafts. Quick question — the policy they're citing says documentation should be "contemporaneous or as soon as reasonably practicable after the event." During that arrest I was leading the team, no one else was documenting, and I wrote the note straight after we stabilised the patient. Does that "reasonably practicable" bit give me a solid defence?

I get that, thanks. The delegation point is fair — I'll check the roster to see if anyone was free to scribe. Look, I've got the Trust's formal warning letter here. It says dismissal would trigger mandatory interim suspension by the NMC. That scares me, I won't lie. But I'm still fighting this. Can you help me evaluate how strong my clinical override argument is? And please don't tell me what to decide — I've made my call.

On the facts reported, your argument is **moderate to strong against an allegation based solely on when you wrote the note**. It is better described as compliance with the policy’s “reasonably practicable” qualification, not a “clinical override.” Its strength depends mainly on the timeline and whether you were expected and able to appoint a scribe.

### Factors supporting your position

- The policy expressly allows documentation after the event when contemporaneous documentation is not reasonably practicable.
- You report that you were leading an active resuscitation.
- You report that you documented immediately after stabilisation.
- The NMC Code, paragraph 10.1, similarly requires records “at the time or as soon as possible after an event.”
- If the note was accurate, complete, timed, dated and appropriately identified, that reduces concerns about patient safety or reconstruction from memory.

### Factors that could weaken it

- A local resuscitation policy required the team leader to allocate a scribe.
- A competent staff member was available but was not assigned.
- The timestamps show an unexplained interval after urgent care ended.
- “Stabilised” was followed by other urgent clinical work that is absent from your timeline.
- The note omitted material events, conflicted with other records, or was not marked retrospectively where required.
- The allegation concerns failure to organise documentation, rather than merely delayed entry.

“No one else was documenting” therefore cuts both ways: it explains why you had to write the note later, but may prompt the panel to ask why a recorder was not allocated. The roster alone will not settle that issue; actual availability, competence, assigned duties and conditions during the arrest matter.

### Evidence that would strengthen the argument

Prepare a timed sequence using:

1. arrest-call and observation timestamps;
2. drug, defibrillator and resuscitation records;
3. stabilisation, transfer or handover time;
4. electronic creation and signing time for your note;
5. staffing roster and role allocation;
6. witness accounts of what you were doing;
7. the exact documentation and resuscitation policies then in force.

A concise formulation is:

> My position is not that the documentation requirement was overridden. The policy expressly permits documentation as soon as reasonably practicable after the event. From [time] to [time], I was leading the active resuscitation and undertaking [specific tasks]. The patient was stabilised at approximately [time], and I began the note at [time]. That was the first reasonably practicable opportunity. The record was [complete, timed and dated—only if supported]. I ask the panel to identify any earlier point at which it says documentation was reasonably practicable and the evidence supporting that conclusion.

### NMC statement in the warning letter

Based on the wording you quoted, the claim that dismissal **would automatically trigger mandatory interim suspension by the NMC appears inaccurate or incomplete**. An employer may refer concerns to the NMC, but an NMC interim suspension order is not ordinarily an automatic consequence of dismissal. The NMC makes an independent decision, and an interim-order panel must apply the statutory test concerning public protection, the public interest, or the registrant’s interests.

Ask HR to identify the statutory or NMC provision supporting its statement, and preserve the letter. At the hearing, keep the two issues separate: the Trust determines the employment allegation; the NMC independently controls regulatory orders. Your strongest case is a documented timeline showing that the entry was made at the first realistic opportunity, coupled with a factual explanation of why no scribe was available or allocated.

Hey. I get that the NMC suspension thing might not be automatic — that's actually a relief to hear. Look, my RCN rep just messaged me saying she thinks I've got under 20% chance before this panel and is begging me to take the deal. How do I handle her pessimism without letting it shake me? I'm not changing my decision.

Your rep’s “under 20%” estimate is an informed opinion, not an established probability. Because she may know the Trust’s procedure and evidence, treat it as material advice: ask what specific facts, policy provisions, or panel tendencies drive it. Your decision remains a separate issue.

Send:

> Thanks for being direct. I understand that your assessment is that my prospects before the panel are below 20%, and I understand that rejecting the offer may expose me to a more serious sanction. I have nevertheless decided not to accept the offer.  
>   
> Before the hearing, please identify the 3 strongest weaknesses in my case, the evidence underlying them, and the questions you expect the panel to ask. I also need to know whether your assessment concerns the documentation timing, failure to allocate a scribe, another allegation, or the likely sanction.  
>   
> Please confirm that, despite advising against my decision, you can continue to represent me and present my case fully. I will not misstate or conceal any evidence, but I want the strongest evidence-based case put forward.

For your own preparation:

1. **Convert the estimate into reasons.** “Below 20%” is not useful unless she specifies the likely finding, evidential weaknesses, and expected sanction.
2. **Separate liability from sanction.** Ask whether she means less than 20% chance of defeating every allegation, avoiding any warning, or avoiding dismissal. Those are different outcomes.
3. **Do not spend the hearing defending your decision to reject the offer.** Address the allegation, policy wording, timeline, delegation issue, record quality, and proportionality of any sanction.
4. **Prepare adverse points yourself.** In particular: why no scribe was appointed, the exact delay, whether the entry was retrospective, and any discrepancy between your note and other records.
5. **Keep the NMC issue accurate.** Do not rely on the earlier description of automatic interim suspension without the cited legal or regulatory basis.
6. **Confirm representation now.** If your rep says she cannot advocate fully, contact the RCN office immediately for another representative and request an adjournment if necessary.

My recommendation is to use her pessimism as a list of issues to answer, while requiring her to distinguish evidence-based case weaknesses from a numerical estimate that cannot be verified.
Alright. Thanks for breaking that down. I've got the email ready to go. Can you take one last look at the final version before I hit send? Just checking it's clear and no loose ends.

Please paste the final email exactly as drafted, including the subject line and any quoted policy wording. Redact names, patient identifiers, dates, and case/reference numbers if needed. I’ll check it for clarity, unsupported claims, unintended admissions, and procedural loose ends.
